definition: A regulated market is served by a single government-sanctioned monopoly utility overseen by a public utility/service commission, while a deregulated market is coordinated by an RTO/ISO and open to any party that builds and connects generation to the grid.
core_idea: Regulated markets control utility behavior through legislative rate cases that approve spending (with profit tied to a percentage of approved spend), whereas deregulated markets rely on competitive auctions, guaranteed equal transmission access, and economic incentives; most energy trading activity occurs in deregulated markets.
key_points: In regulated markets, the monopoly utility typically owns generation, transmission lines, and maintenance infrastructure.
A public utility/service commission approves utility spending in annual rate case hearings; utility profit is a percentage of approved spending.
In deregulated markets, any party can own a power plant and connect it to the grid to sell power.
Deregulated markets guarantee equal transmission access to all participants and favor economic/competitive innovation.
Regulated markets rely on legislative mandates; deregulated markets rely on economic incentives.
Most energy trading occurs in deregulated markets.
relationships: Sets up the daily auction / marginal pricing mechanic that applies specifically in deregulated markets
trading_implications: Competitive price discovery, and therefore trading opportunity, is concentrated in deregulated markets rather than regulated monopoly territories.
Utility profit tied to approved capital spending (regulated markets) creates a different incentive structure than the competitive returns available in deregulated markets.
caveats: Deregulation does not mean an absence of oversight — it replaces legislative/rate-case control with auction-based, economically incentivized coordination.
